rules.title: System Integrity Protection is disabled
rules.summary: System Integrity Protection stops any software, even with your admin password, from changing macOS system files. With it off, malware can hide inside the system and survive updates.
rules.remedy: Restart into Recovery (hold the power button on Apple silicon), open Terminal from the Utilities menu, run csrutil enable, then restart.

rules.title: Gatekeeper is disabled
rules.summary: Gatekeeper blocks apps that aren't from the App Store or an identified, notarized developer. With it off, any downloaded app can run without a warning.
rules.remedy: Open Terminal and run sudo spctl --global-enable, then check System Settings › Privacy & Security allows apps from the App Store and identified developers.

rules.title: Application Firewall is disabled
rules.summary: The Application Firewall blocks incoming connections to apps you haven't allowed. With it off, any service on your Mac can be reached from the network you're on.
rules.remedy: Open System Settings › Network › Firewall and turn it on.

rules.title: Launch item downloads and runs a remote script
rules.summary: A launch item starts automatically and fetches code from the internet to run it. This is the most common way malware installs itself and updates.
rules.remedy: Show the plist in Finder. If you don't know what installed it, run launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u) <path> for a LaunchAgent (or sudo launchctl bootout system <path> for a LaunchDaemon), move the file to the Trash, and restart.

rules.title: Launch item runs a program from a temp or shared folder
rules.summary: Real apps don't start programs from temporary or shared folders. Malware drops its program there because every user can write to them.
rules.remedy: Show the plist in Finder, unload it with launchctl bootout, then move the plist and the program it points to into the Trash.

rules.title: Launch item runs an inline script
rules.summary: The launch item runs a script written directly in its settings instead of a real app. Installers rarely do this; adware and malware often do.
rules.remedy: Read the command in the finding. If it isn't from software you installed on purpose, unload it with launchctl bootout and move the plist to the Trash.

rules.title: Shell startup file runs remote or hidden code
rules.summary: This line runs every time you open Terminal and downloads code from the internet, or decodes hidden code, and runs it.
rules.remedy: Open the file in a text editor (open -e <file>), delete the line, save, and open a new Terminal window.

rules.title: Shell startup file injects a library into every program
rules.summary: DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES loads extra code into every program started from your shell. Attackers use it to spy on commands and steal credentials.
rules.remedy: Open the file in a text editor, delete the DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES line, save, and open a new Terminal window.

rules.title: Reverse shell is running
rules.summary: A process is connecting a shell back to another computer. Whoever is on the other side can type commands on your Mac right now.
rules.remedy: Disconnect from the network, quit the process in Activity Monitor, then scan again to find the launch item or cron job that started it. Change your passwords from another device.

rules.title: Cryptocurrency miner is running
rules.summary: A cryptocurrency miner is running. Unless you started it, someone is using your Mac's power for their profit, and it usually arrives with other malware.
rules.remedy: Quit it in Activity Monitor, then scan again to find and remove the launch item that starts it.

rules.title: Mass network scanner is running (worm spreading)
rules.summary: A tool that scans large parts of the internet or your network is running. Worms use these to find their next victims.
rules.remedy: If you didn't start it, quit it in Activity Monitor and look for the launch item that started it.

rules.title: Cron job downloads or runs hidden code
rules.summary: A scheduled job downloads or decodes code and runs it on a timer, so malware keeps coming back.
rules.remedy: Run crontab -e in Terminal, delete the line, and save.

rules.title: Port commonly used by backdoors is listening
rules.summary: A program is listening on a port that backdoors and hacking tools use by default. Others on your network may be able to connect to it.
rules.remedy: The finding shows which program has the port open. If you don't recognize it, quit it and remove whatever starts it.

rules.title: IRC port used by botnets and worms is listening
rules.summary: Botnets and worms use IRC ports to receive commands. A listener here can mean your Mac is part of one.
rules.remedy: Quit the program shown in the finding unless you run an IRC server on purpose.

rules.title: Remote access service is on
rules.summary: Remote Login (SSH) or Screen Sharing is on. That's fine if you use it, but it lets others on your network try to log in.
rules.remedy: If you don't use it, turn off Remote Login and Screen Sharing in System Settings › General › Sharing. Otherwise ignore this finding.

rules.title: Silver Sparrow malware files
rules.summary: Silver Sparrow is a macOS malware family that checks in with its servers every hour and can download and run anything its authors send.
rules.remedy: Move the files listed to the Trash, unload the launch agents with launchctl bootout, and restart.

rules.title: EvilQuest (ThiefQuest) ransomware files
rules.summary: EvilQuest encrypts your files for ransom, steals files and records keystrokes.
rules.remedy: Disconnect from the network, unload the launch item with launchctl bootout, move the files to the Trash, and restore encrypted files from a backup.

rules.title: KeRanger ransomware files
rules.summary: KeRanger is ransomware that arrived inside a hacked Transmission installer and encrypts your documents.
rules.remedy: Move the files to the Trash, delete the infected app, and restore encrypted files from a backup.

rules.title: Keydnap backdoor files
rules.summary: Keydnap is a backdoor that steals passwords from your keychain and lets attackers control your Mac.
rules.remedy: Unload and delete the launch agent and the icloudsyncd file, then change the passwords stored in your keychain from another device.

rules.title: FruitFly backdoor files
rules.summary: FruitFly is a backdoor that can take screenshots, turn on the camera and log keystrokes.
rules.remedy: Unload the launch agent, move ~/.client and the plist to the Trash, and restart.

rules.title: Proton remote access trojan files
rules.summary: Proton is a remote access trojan spread through a hacked video player installer. It steals passwords, keychains and browser data.
rules.remedy: Delete the files and the infected app, then change your passwords from another device.

rules.title: EICAR antivirus test file (harmless, used to test the scanner)
rules.summary: This is the EICAR test file, which every antivirus treats as a threat on purpose. It is harmless and only proves the scanner works.
rules.remedy: Move it to the Trash when you're done testing.

rules.title: Launch item starts an unsigned or tampered program
rules.summary: Software that starts by itself at login or boot is almost always signed by its developer. An unsigned, ad-hoc signed or modified program here is how most macOS malware keeps itself running.
rules.remedy: Show the launch item in Finder and look up the program it starts. If you didn't install it, unload it with launchctl bootout, move the plist and the program to the Trash, and restart.

rules.title: App is unsigned or its signature is broken
rules.summary: Gatekeeper would refuse to open this app, so it runs only because Gatekeeper was bypassed. Cracked and trojanized apps look like this, and so do apps whose files changed after the developer signed them.
rules.remedy: If you didn't build it yourself or knowingly allow it, delete the app and download it again from the developer or the App Store. If an app updates itself into this state, reinstalling it fixes the signature.

rules.title: Atomic Stealer (AMOS) backdoor files
rules.summary: Atomic Stealer is the most widespread macOS stealer. It takes passwords, browser data and crypto wallets, and newer versions leave a backdoor that restarts itself and takes commands every minute. Assume your passwords, browser sessions and crypto wallets were stolen.
rules.remedy: Disconnect from the network. Run sudo launchctl bootout system /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.finder.helper.plist, delete the plist and the hidden .helper, .agent and .mainhelper files in your home folder, and restart. From another device, change your Apple Account, email and banking passwords, sign out of other sessions, and move any crypto to a new wallet.

rules.title: CrashStealer files
rules.summary: CrashStealer poses as Apple's crash reporter, asks for your password, copies your keychain and browser data, and starts again at every login. Assume your passwords, browser sessions and crypto wallets were stolen.
rules.remedy: Run launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.crashreporter.helper.plist, delete the files listed, and restart. From another device, change your Apple Account, email and banking passwords, sign out of other sessions, and move any crypto to a new wallet.

rules.title: ClickLock stealer and GSocket backdoor files
rules.summary: ClickLock arrives through fake 'paste this into Terminal' instructions. It steals browser data and installs a GSocket backdoor disguised as iCloud that gives attackers a remote shell. Assume your passwords, browser sessions and crypto wallets were stolen.
rules.remedy: Unload both launch agents with launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u) <plist>, delete the files listed, and restart. From another device, change your Apple Account, email and banking passwords, sign out of other sessions, and move any crypto to a new wallet.

rules.title: Sapphire Sleet (North Korea) backdoor files
rules.summary: Sapphire Sleet is a North Korean group that targets crypto and finance workers with fake Zoom and Teams updates. Its backdoors run as fake Google and Apple services and steal credentials and wallets.
rules.remedy: Treat this Mac as compromised: disconnect it, back up only your documents, erase and reinstall macOS, then change every password from a clean device. Report it to your security team if this is a work Mac.

rules.title: ICMacOS (Icarus) stealer files
rules.summary: ICMacOS steals credentials and keeps remote access through a launch agent with an Apple-like name. Assume your passwords, browser sessions and crypto wallets were stolen.
rules.remedy: Run launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.systemupdater.plist, delete the files listed, and restart. From another device, change your Apple Account, email and banking passwords, sign out of other sessions, and move any crypto to a new wallet.

rules.title: Launch item pretends to be part of macOS
rules.summary: Apple's own launch items live only in /System, which nothing else can write to. A com.apple.* launch item in your Library or /Library was put there by something else, which is how several 2026 stealers hide.
rules.remedy: Show the plist in Finder and look at the program it starts. Unless you know which app installed it, unload it with launchctl bootout and move the plist and its program to the Trash.

rules.title: Stealer is collecting or uploading data right now
rules.summary: A running process is doing what macOS stealers do: zipping your data into a temporary folder and uploading it, showing a fake password prompt, or running a downloaded AppleScript.
rules.remedy: Disconnect from the network now, quit the process in Activity Monitor, and scan again to find what started it. From another device, change your Apple Account, email and banking passwords, sign out of other sessions, and move any crypto to a new wallet.

rules.title: Stealer backdoor is running
rules.summary: A process matching a known stealer backdoor is running (AMOS's hidden .helper or .agent loop, or ClickLock's fake SystemUIServer). Attackers can send it commands.
rules.remedy: Disconnect from the network, then follow the steps for the matching malware files finding. Killing the process alone isn't enough; AMOS restarts it within a second.

rules.title: SSH key can log in to your Mac
rules.summary: Anyone holding the private half of this key can log in as you without a password whenever Remote Login is on. Attackers add their own key here to keep access even after you change your password.
rules.remedy: If you added this key yourself, ignore this finding; a new key will still show up. Otherwise delete its line from ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, and turn off Remote Login in System Settings › General › Sharing if you don't use it.

rules.title: Profile controls your proxy, DNS, certificates or browser
rules.summary: This configuration profile can route your traffic through someone else's proxy or DNS, trust their certificate so they can read encrypted traffic, or force browser settings and extensions. Adware and spyware install profiles like this because they survive deleting the app.
rules.remedy: Unless your school or company installed it, remove it in System Settings › General › Device Management, then check your browser's search engine and extensions.

rules.title: Configuration profile is installed
rules.summary: Configuration profiles change system settings and are normally installed only by schools and companies. This one is listed so you know it's there.
rules.remedy: If you recognize it, ignore this finding. Otherwise remove it in System Settings › General › Device Management.

rules.title: Browser extension not from an official store
rules.summary: This extension updates from somewhere other than the Chrome Web Store, Edge Add-ons or Mozilla, or isn't signed by Mozilla. Malware installs extensions this way to read your browsing, steal sessions and swap search results, because store review can't stop it.
rules.remedy: Remove it from the browser's extensions page. If it keeps coming back, look for a configuration profile or launch item that reinstalls it (Bluehat checks both), then change passwords for sites you used while it was installed.

rules.title: Browser extension can read cookies on every site
rules.summary: With cookie access on every site, this extension could take over any account you're signed in to. Many honest extensions ask for this, but it's the permission session-stealing extensions need.
rules.remedy: Keep it only if you trust the developer and use it. Otherwise remove it, or limit it to specific sites in the browser's extension settings.

rules.title: Browser extension can debug pages or reroute traffic
rules.summary: The debugger permission lets an extension read and change everything on a page, including passwords as you type them. The proxy permission lets it send all your browsing through another server. VPN and developer tools need these; malicious extensions abuse them.
rules.remedy: Keep it only if it's a VPN or developer tool you installed on purpose. Otherwise remove it.
